AWOL stands for Absent Without Leave. When someone is described as AWOL, it means they have disappeared from a place where they were expected or required to be, without asking for or receiving permission to leave.

The word "leave" here doesn't mean "to leave a place." It means official permission to be away — like when an employee gets approved time off. So "without leave" = without permission.
Where It Comes From (Conceptually, Not Historically)

Think of it this way: imagine you have a responsibility — a duty, a job, a role — that requires you to be somewhere. Now imagine you simply vanish. No explanation. No approval. No warning. That is the heart of what AWOL means.
The Military Meaning (Its Strict, Original Use)

In its most precise and serious sense, AWOL is a military term. A soldier is AWOL when they leave their unit, post, or assigned location without getting official permission from a commanding officer.

This is not the same as being late, or taking a short break. An AWOL soldier has completely walked away from their duty — sometimes for hours, sometimes for days or even permanently — without authorization.

In the military, going AWOL is a punishable offense. It is treated seriously because a soldier's absence can directly affect the safety and effectiveness of their entire unit. The military distinguishes between being AWOL (absent for a limited, undefined time) and desertion (abandoning duty with no intention of ever returning), though in common speech, the two ideas are often blurred.

So when someone in the military is described as AWOL, it carries a strong sense of breach of duty — not just being absent, but being absent in a way that is unauthorized and irresponsible.

Over time, AWOL escaped the military and entered ordinary everyday language. Now it is widely used to describe any person (not just a soldier) who has gone missing from somewhere they were expected to be — without explanation or permission.

This informal use is very flexible. You can use it whenever someone has:

  • Vanished without notice
  • Stopped showing up
  • Become unreachable
  • Abandoned a role or responsibility unexpectedly

Examples:

  • "Our project manager has been AWOL all week — nobody can reach him."
  • "The team captain went AWOL right before the tournament."
  • "She's been AWOL from family dinners ever since she moved to the city."

In all of these cases, the person is absent, unaccountable, and without a valid or communicated reason. The word quietly signals that their absence is not okay — that someone or something is suffering because of it.
The Feeling and Tone the Word Carries

This is important: AWOL is not a neutral word. It carries a clear negative connotation. When you call someone AWOL, you are implying:

  • They had a responsibility to be somewhere or to someone.
  • They failed that responsibility.
  • Their absence was unexplained and unauthorized.
  • People are affected — left waiting, confused, or let down.

It is subtly accusatory. Saying someone is AWOL is stronger than simply saying they are "absent" or "missing." It frames their absence as a kind of abandonment — a failure of duty, whether that duty is a military post, a job, a team, or even a relationship.
A Key Distinction: AWOL vs. Just Being Absent

Not every absence is AWOL. If your coworker is sick and called in, they are absent — but not AWOL. If your friend is on vacation and told everyone in advance, they are away — but not AWOL. AWOL specifically requires two things working together:

  1. Absence — the person is not where they should be.
  2. No permission or explanation — no one approved it, and no one was told why.

Remove either of those two elements, and the word no longer applies.
Can It Apply to Things, Not Just People?

Yes, loosely. In informal speech, people sometimes use AWOL to describe things that have disappeared or are missing when they're needed:

  • "My motivation has gone completely AWOL this week."
  • "The instruction manual is AWOL — I can't find it anywhere."

This is a playful, metaphorical extension of the word, and perfectly acceptable in casual conversation.

AWOL describes someone (or something) that is missing from where they are supposed to be, without permission or explanation — carrying a clear implication that their absence is a failure of responsibility.
